redirect_from:   - /education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/online-ide-integrations ---  ### About integration with an online IDE  {% data reusables.classroom.about-online-ides %}   After a student accepts an assignment with an online IDE, the README file in the student's assignment repository will contain a button to open the assignment in the IDE. The student can begin working immediately, and no additional configuration is necessary.  ![Button for online IDE in README.md for assignment repository](/assets/images/help/classroom/assignment-repository-ide-button-in-readme.png)  ### Supported online IDEs  {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} supports the following online IDEs. You can learn more about the student experience for each IDE.  | IDE | More information | | :- | :- | | Microsoft MakeCode Arcade | "[About using MakeCode Arcade with {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %}](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/about-using-makecode-arcade-with-github-classroom)" | | Repl.it | "[About using Repl.it with GitHub Classroom](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/about-using-replit-with-github-classroom)" |  ### Configuring an online IDE for an assignment  You can choose the online IDE you'd like to use for an assignment when you create an assignment. To learn how to create a new assignment that uses an online IDE, see "[Create an individual assignment](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/create-an-individual-assignment)" or "[Create a group assignment](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/create-a-group-assignment)."  ### Authorizing the OAuth app for an online IDE  The first time you configure an assignment with an online IDE, you must authorize the OAuth app for the online IDE for your organization.  !["Go grant access" button in popover for authorizing OAuth app for online IDE](/assets/images/help/classroom/assignment-ide-go-grant-access-button.png)  For all repositories, grant the app **read** access to metadata, administration, and code, and **write** access to administration and code. For more information, see "[Authorizing OAuth Apps](/github/authenticating-to-github/authorizing-oauth-apps)."  ### Further reading  - "[About READMEs](/github/creating-cloning-and-archiving-repositories/about-readmes)"  7  ...ducation/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/learn-with-github-classroom.md  @@ -0,0 +1,7 @@ --- title: Learn with GitHub Classroom intro: You can participate in coursework in {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} and see results from your teacher. mapTopic: true versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  33  ...on/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/leave-feedback-with-pull-requests.md  @@ -0,0 +1,33 @@ --- title: Leave feedback with pull requests intro: You can leave feedback for your students in a special pull request within the repository for each assignment. permissions: People with read permissions to a repository can leave feedback in a pull request for the repository. versions:   free-pro-team: '*' redirect_from:   - /education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/leaving-feedback-in-github ---  ### About feedback pull requests for assignments  {% data reusables.classroom.you-can-create-a-pull-request-for-feedback %}  When you enable the pull request for feedback for an assignment, {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} will create a special pull request titled **Feedback** in the assignment repository for each student or team. The pull request automatically shows every commit that a student pushed to the assignment repository's default branch.  ### Prerequisites  To create and access the feedback pull request, you must enable the feedback pull request when you create the assignment. {% data reusables.classroom.for-more-information-about-assignment-creation %}  ### Leaving feedback in a pull request for an assignment  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} 1. In the list of classrooms, click the classroom with the assignment you want to review.   ![Classroom in list of classrooms for an organization](/assets/images/help/classroom/click-classroom-in-list.png) {% data reusables.classroom.click-assignment-in-list %} 1. To the right of the submission, click **Review**.   ![Review button for assignment in list of submissions for an assignment](/assets/images/help/classroom/assignments-click-review-button.png) 1. Review the pull request. For more information, see "[Commenting on a pull request](/github/collaborating-with-issues-and-pull-requests/commenting-on-a-pull-request)."  ### Further reading  - "[Integrate {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} with an IDE](http://localhost:4000/en/free-pro-team@latest/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/integrate-github-classroom-with-an-ide)"  121  content/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/manage-classrooms.md  @@ -0,0 +1,121 @@ --- title: Manage classrooms intro: You can create and manage a classroom for each course that you teach using {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %}. permissions: Organization owners can manage a classroom for an organization. versions:   free-pro-team: '*' redirect_from:   - /education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/archive-a-classroom ---  ### About classrooms  {% data reusables.classroom.about-classrooms %}  ![Classroom](/assets/images/help/classroom/classroom-hero.png)  ### About management of classrooms  {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} uses organization accounts on {% data variables.product.product_name %} to manage permissions, administration, and security for each classroom that you create. Each organization can have multiple classrooms.  After you create a classroom, {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} will prompt you to invite teaching assistants (TAs) and admins to the classroom. Each classroom can have one or more admins. Admins can be teachers, TAs, or any other course administrator who you'd like to have control over your classrooms on {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %}.  Invite TAs and admins to your classroom by inviting the user accounts on {% data variables.product.product_name %} to your organization as organization owners and sharing the URL for your classrom. Organization owners can administer any classroom for the organization. For more information, see "[Permission levels for an organization](/github/setting-up-and-managing-organizations-and-teams/permission-levels-for-an-organization)" and "[Inviting users to join your organization](/github/setting-up-and-managing-organizations-and-teams/inviting-users-to-join-your-organization)."  When you're done using a classroom, you can archive the classroom and refer to the classroom, roster, and assignments later, or you can delete the classroom if you no longer need the classroom.  ### About classroom rosters  Each classroom has a roster. A roster is a list of identifiers for the students who participate in your course.  When you first share the URL for an assignment with a student, the student must sign into {% data variables.product.product_name %} with a user account to link the user account to an identifier for the classroom. After the student links a user account, you can see the associated user account in the roster. You can also see when the student accepts or submits an assignment.  ![Classroom roster](/assets/images/help/classroom/roster-hero.png)  ### Prerequisites  You must have an organization account on {% data variables.product.product_name %} to manage classrooms on {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %}. For more information, see "[Types of {% data variables.product.company_short %} accounts](/github/getting-started-with-github/types-of-github-accounts#organization-accounts)" and "[Creating a new organization from scratch](/github/setting-up-and-managing-organizations-and-teams/creating-a-new-organization-from-scratch)."  You must authorize the OAuth app for {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} for your organization to manage classrooms for your organization account. For more information, see "[Authorizing OAuth Apps](/github/authenticating-to-github/authorizing-oauth-apps)."  ### Creating a classroom  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} 1. Click **New classroom**.   !["New classroom" button](/assets/images/help/classroom/click-new-classroom-button.png) {% data reusables.classroom.guide-create-new-classroom %}  After you create a classroom, you can begin creating assignments for students. For more information, see "[Create an individual assignment](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/create-an-individual-assignment)" or "[Create a group assignment](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/create-a-group-assignment)."  ### Creating a roster for your classroom  You can create a roster of the students who participate in your course.  If your course already has a roster, you can update the students on the roster or delete the roster. For more information, see "[Adding a student to the roster for your classroom](#adding-students-to-the-roster-for-your-classroom)" or "[Deleting a roster for a classroom](#deleting-a-roster-for-a-classroom)."  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-classroom-in-list %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-students %} 1. To connect {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %} to your LMS and import a roster, click {% octicon "mortar-board" aria-label="The mortar board icon" %} **Import from a learning management system** and follow the instructions. For more information, see "[Connect a learning management system to {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %}](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/connect-a-learning-management-system-to-github-classroom)."     !["Import from a learning management system" button](/assets/images/help/classroom/click-import-from-a-learning-management-system-button.png) 1. To create a roster manually, type your student identifiers. Optionally, click **Upload a CSV or text file** to upload a file containing the identifiers.     ![Text field for typing student identifiers and "Upload a CSV or text file" button](/assets/images/help/classroom/type-or-upload-student-identifiers.png) 1. Click **Create roster**.   !["Create roster" button](/assets/images/help/classroom/click-create-roster-button.png)  ### Adding students to the roster for your classroom  Your classroom must have an existing roster to add students to the roster. For more information about creating a roster, see "[Creating a roster for your classrom](#creating-a-roster-for-your-classroom)."  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-classroom-in-list %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-students %} 1. To the right of "Classroom roster", click **Update students**.   !["Update students" button to the right of "Classroom roster" heading above list of students](/assets/images/help/classroom/click-update-students-button.png) 1. Follow the instructions to add students to the roster.     - To import students from an LMS, click **Sync from a learning management system**. For more information about importing a roster from an LMS, see "[Connect a learning management system to {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %}](/education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/connect-a-learning-management-system-to-github-classroom)."     - To manually add students, under "Manually add students", click **Upload a CSV or text file** or type the identifiers for the students, then click **Add roster entries**.       ![Modal for choosing method of adding students to classroom](/assets/images/help/classroom/classroom-add-students-to-your-roster.png)  ### Renaming a classroom  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-classroom-in-list %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-settings %} 1. Under "Classroom name", type a new name for the classroom.   ![Text field under "Classroom name" for typing classroom name](/assets/images/help/classroom/settings-type-classroom-name.png) 1. Click **Rename classroom**.   !["Rename classroom" button](/assets/images/help/classroom/settings-click-rename-classroom-button.png)  ### Archiving or unarchiving a classroom  You can archive a classroom that you no longer use on {% data variables.product.prodname_classroom %}. When you archive a classroom, you can't create new assignments or edit existing assignments for the classroom. Students can't accept invitations to assignments in archived classrooms.  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} 1. To the right of a classroom's name, select the {% octicon "kebab-horizontal" aria-label="The horizontal kebab icon" %} drop-down menu, then click **Archive**.   ![Drop-down menu from horizontal kebab icon and "Archive" menu item](/assets/images/help/classroom/use-drop-down-then-click-archive.png) 1. To unarchive a classroom, to the right of a classroom's name, select the {% octicon "kebab-horizontal" aria-label="The horizontal kebab icon" %} drop-down menu, then click **Unarchive**.   ![Drop-down menu from horizontal kebab icon and "Unarchive" menu item](/assets/images/help/classroom/use-drop-down-then-click-unarchive.png)  ### Deleting a roster for a classroom  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-classroom-in-list %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-students %} 1. Under "Delete this roster", click **Delete roster**.   !["Delete roster" button under "Delete this roster" in "Students" tab for a classroom](/assets/images/help/classroom/students-click-delete-roster-button.png) 1. Read the warnings, then click **Delete roster**.   !["Delete roster" button under "Delete this roster" in "Students" tab for a classroom](/assets/images/help/classroom/students-click-delete-roster-button-in-modal.png)  ### Deleting a classroom  {% data reusables.classroom.sign-into-github-classroom %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-classroom-in-list %} {% data reusables.classroom.click-settings %} 1. To the right of "Delete this classroom", click **Delete classroom**.   !["Delete repository" button](/assets/images/help/classroom/click-delete-classroom-button.png) 1. **Read the warnings**. 1. To verify that you're deleting the correct classroom, type the name of the classroom you want to delete.   ![Modal for deleting a classrom with warnings and text field for classroom name](/assets/images/help/classroom/delete-classroom-modal-with-warning.png) 1. Click **Delete classroom**.   !["Delete classroom" button](/assets/images/help/classroom/delete-classroom-click-delete-classroom-button.png)  22  ...on/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/run-student-code-in-an-online-ide.md  @@ -0,0 +1,22 @@ --- title: Run student code in an online IDE intro: You can run the code from a student assignment within the online integrated development environment (IDE) that you configured for the assignment. versions:   free-pro-team: '*' redirect_from:   - /education/manage-coursework-with-github-classroom/running-student-code ---  ### About student code and online IDEs  If you configure an online integrated development environment (IDE) for an assignment, you can run the code within the online IDE. **Product Description Text**:
> GitOps-managed homelab using Kubernetes (Talos), ArgoCD, and Terraform for infrastructure as code.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Eden is a personal Kubernetes homelab built by an infrastructure professional to experiment with tools and patterns beyond production constraints. Terraform provisions Talos Linux VMs on a three-node Proxmox cluster, after which everything is delivered through GitOps: GitHub Actions build container images, Kargo promotes them from stage to prod, and Argo CD reconciles the cluster to the desired state. The stack runs self-hosted services like a blog, portfolio, media stack, and AI workloads, with Traefik (Gateway API) handling ingress, External Secrets Operator sourcing credentials from Bitwarden, cert-manager issuing TLS, and external-dns managing Cloudflare records. KEDA with the HTTP add-on lets nine idle apps scale to zero and wake on the first request, while Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and Tempo provide full observability. Security is layered with Falco's eBPF runtime detection and automated Trivy vulnerability scans uploaded to GitHub Security. It's a useful reference for platform engineers, SREs, and homelab enthusiasts who want to study a production-grade GitOps setup with modern Kubernetes tooling.

- **Attached Keywords**: `frontend, github, developer-tools, open-source, tools, llm, vite, react`

**Product Description Text**:
> GitDeepSearch is a React-based web application that lets users find GitHub repositories and developers using plain natural language instead of GitHub's native query syntax. It offers two search modes: Quick Search, which translates everyday phrases into GitHub's query language with automatic detection of 20+ programming languages and frameworks, and Deep Search, which runs four parallel strategies—relevance, stars, recent activity, and README content—merging and deduplicating results for higher-quality matches. The natural language engine maps phrases like "fitness mobile app in Flutter" to GitHub qualifiers such as `language:dart`, while rich result cards surface stars, forks, topics, bios, and follower counts. Because it operates entirely client-side and talks directly to the GitHub Search API, no backend is required, making it easy to deploy on GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or Docker. Built with React 18, Vite 5, and React Router 6, it includes CI/CD workflows for automated testing and deployment, targeting developers, recruiters, and open-source contributors who want a faster, more intuitive way to discover code and talent on GitHub.

**Product Description Text**:
> Pagecast publishes it instantly to a shareable Cloudflare pages URL straight from your terminal or coding agent. Claude code builds a dashboard, runs one command, hands you a live link hosted free on Cloudflare's edge

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Pagecast is a local-first publishing tool for sharing HTML reports, Markdown docs, and static mini apps to shareable Cloudflare Pages URLs. It bridges the gap between local development and public sharing by letting developers preview content locally, then push it to Cloudflare with a single CLI command or via coding agents like Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor. The tool ships a local admin UI for managing publications plus headless `pagecast` commands for automation, supporting features like memorable unlisted slugs, expiry windows, password protection enforced via Cloudflare Pages Functions, and revocable share links. Every publish creates an immutable deployment with its own snapshot URL, and optional analytics (via a Worker + D1) provide view counts and referrer data without storing raw IPs. Built on Node.js 20.19+, Pagecast wraps Wrangler for Cloudflare OAuth, runs on macOS as a login service with a `pagecast.localhost` redirect, and exposes an MCP server for AI agents — making it well suited for developer-facing workflows where agents generate artifacts that need quick, controlled public URLs.

- **Attached Keywords**: `security, devops, rust`

**Product Description Text**:
> `cargo-frisk` is a security tool for Rust developers that intercepts the gap between what `git` tracks and what `cargo package` actually publishes to crates.io. It solves the problem of untracked secrets—`.env` files, stray credential files, debug keys—slipping into crates because traditional secret scanners only read the repository, not the tarball. The tool diffs `git ls-files` against the packaged `.crate` archive, highlighting files that go out the door without ever being tracked, then applies secret-detection rules (adapted from gitleaks) to the packaged contents. Features include built-in mitigations for false positives (severity threshold, entropy gate, path context for test/fixture directories, inline `frisk:allow` suppression), three distinct exit codes, SARIF output for GitHub Code Scanning, and a library API for programmatic use. Configuration lives in `Cargo.toml` under `[package.metadata.frisk]` or `[workspace.metadata.frisk]`, with overridable and accumulative keys. It targets Rust library authors and CI pipelines, is distributed via `cargo install` or `cargo binstall`, ships with a prebuilt GitHub Action, and is written in Rust with an MSRV of 1.85 under dual MIT/Apache-2.0 licensing.

It addresses the gap left by schema-only checkers like `mcp-server-diff` and the Inspector's CLI by actually invoking tools and comparing results against a saved baseline, causing the build to fail when outputs get worse. Users define test cases in a `golden_set.yaml` file specifying tool calls and expected outputs, then run `mcp-eval-gate run --update-baseline` once to record the baseline and `mcp-eval-gate run` on subsequent CI runs to gate against regressions. The tool supports three matching modes—`exact`, `contains`, and `judge` (LLM-scored against a rubric with a configurable threshold)—and can target both stdio and HTTP MCP servers. Built in Python 3.12+ and distributed via PyPI, it also exposes itself as an MCP server (`mcp-eval-gate-mcp`) so agents can invoke the gate directly. The package includes validation runs against real servers, including catching a genuine UTF-8 boundary bug in the official MCP filesystem server, and is aimed at MCP server maintainers who want meaningful behavioral regression coverage in continuous integration.

The current collection spans 71 scenes across categories like mechanisms, information, and systems, while contribution tools—including a production guide and a reusable AI skill for drafting new scenes—make it straightforward for educators, translators, and developers to extend coverage. Continuous integration through GitHub Actions enforces formatting, types, scene/audio contracts, and production builds before publishing to Cloudflare Workers.

**Product Description Text**:

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Memvid is a single-file, portable AI memory system that packages data, embeddings, search structures, and metadata into one self-contained file, eliminating the need for complex RAG pipelines or server-based vector databases. It organizes memory as an append-only sequence of "Smart Frames"—immutable units with timestamps, checksums, and metadata—enabling crash-safe writes, time-travel debugging, and queries over past memory states. The system delivers sub-5ms local memory access with predictive caching, and benchmarks show +35% accuracy over prior state-of-the-art on the LoCoMo long-horizon conversational recall benchmark, with 0.025ms P50 latency and 1,372× higher throughput than standard approaches. It is built in Rust (`memvid-core`) with optional feature flags for full-text search (BM25 via Tantivy), vector similarity (HNSW + ONNX embeddings), CLIP image search, Whisper audio transcription, PDF extraction, encryption, and temporal reasoning. Memvid ships with SDKs for Rust, and Python, plus a Node.js SDK and CLI, making it suitable for AI agent developers building long-running agents, enterprise knowledge bases, offline-first AI systems, and auditable workflows where persistent, model-agnostic memory is needed.

It treats interactive users and autonomous agents as structurally different loads with separate peak factors and KV requirements, then prices owned hardware, sovereign rentals, and enterprise subscriptions side-by-side while flagging capability gaps. The tool is aimed at platform engineers, IT procurement, and CTOs evaluating private local AI for data-governance reasons, where conventional online comparisons tend to size against the wrong limit or audit-incompatible providers. All calculations run client-side as pure functions in vanilla JavaScript with React + htm loaded via CDN, with no build step, server, or telemetry. Model, hardware, and benchmark data live in editable JSON catalogues, and the engine is covered by Node-based tests that pin its arithmetic against known values.

It solves the problem of AI coding assistants jumping straight into implementation by enforcing a structured workflow: brainstorming requirements into validated designs, isolating work in git worktrees, breaking plans into bite-sized tasks, and executing via subagent-driven development with strict test-driven development (RED-GREEN-REFACTOR). **Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Gentle-AI is a deterministic engineering environment that augments existing AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Codex, and 13 others) with persistent memory, structured workflows, and verifiable evidence of completed work. Its core feature, Engram™, gives agents long-term project context that survives session restarts and context compaction, eliminating the need to re-explain decisions after every break. Organic Driven Development (ODD) scales process to scope—small changes stay lightweight while substantial work gets a single recoverable feature document. Strict TDD enforces failing-test-first behavior when enabled, and Receipt-Driven Development (RDD) provides risk-graded review of finished work, producing a closed-loop audit trail from authorization through implementation to final acknowledgement. The tool is aimed at developers and teams who use AI assistants for code generation but need reliable, reproducible engineering practices rather than ephemeral suggestions. Distributed as a native configuration layer for 17 agent integrations under an MIT license, Gentle-AI targets any user who wants their AI coding partner to accumulate knowledge, follow disciplined workflows, and prove what it did.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> A comprehensive collection of JavaScript implementations of classical algorithms and data structures, organized into well-documented modules covering linked lists, trees, graphs, hash tables, heaps, and advanced structures like Bloom filters, AVL/Red-Black trees, and LRU caches. It includes algorithmic problem-solving examples across categories such as math (Fibonacci, sieve of Eratosthenes, FFT), sets (permutations, knapsack, LCS), strings (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Levenshtein distance), sorting, searching, and graph traversal algorithms. Each entry ships with its own README containing explanations, complexity analysis, links to YouTube walkthroughs, and further reading references, making it both a reference and a learning resource. The project is ideal for computer science students, coding interview preparation, and developers seeking to deepen their understanding of algorithmic fundamentals through clean, executable JavaScript code. Test-driven development is enforced with continuous integration, and the repository supports over a dozen languages for its documentation, reflecting its broad global community of learners.

**Product Description Text**:
> caveman is a Claude Code skill that cuts roughly 65 percent of tokens by talking like a caveman, embracing the idea that fewer tokens often suffice for many tasks. It is aimed at developers who want a fun, pragmatic way to reduce token usage. The skill is positioned as a focused, transparent token-saving trick.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Caveman is a skill/plugin for Claude Code and 30+ AI coding agents that compresses verbose model output into terse, caveman-style replies—cutting output tokens by an average of 65% (ranging 22–87% in benchmarks) without altering code, commands, URLs, or technical accuracy. It solves the problem of bloated AI responses that waste tokens on filler phrases like "I'd be happy to help" while delivering the same actionable information, reducing both cost and time-to-answer for developers. Six compression levels are available (lite, full, ultra, plus wenyan for classical Chinese), switchable mid-session via `/caveman <level>`, with the agent's underlying knowledge and reasoning capacity fully preserved. Beyond simple reply compression, it ships companion tools: `/caveman-commit` for concise commit messages, `/caveman-review` for one-line PR comments, `/caveman-stats` for token-usage tracking, `/caveman-compress` for rewriting memory files (CLAUDE.md, etc.) to save input tokens every future session, and `caveman-shrink` MCP middleware that compresses tool descriptions from any MCP server. Ideal for developers using AI coding assistants who want faster, cheaper, and more scannable responses—installation is a single curl/irm command that auto-detects installed agents, with no configuration needed on Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini where it's enabled by default.

**Product Description Text**:
> Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output, 98% reduction. 12 platforms

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Context Mode is an MCP server that tackles the context window bloat problem faced by AI coding agents, where raw tool outputs (Playwright snapshots, GitHub issues, log files) can consume 40% or more of the available context within minutes. It achieves a 98% reduction in token usage by sandboxing tool outputs, keeping raw data out of the model context while preserving access to computed results. Session continuity is maintained through an SQLite-backed event store indexed with FTS5 and queried via BM25, so agents retain awareness of file edits, tasks, and user decisions across compaction cycles without re-dumping history into context. The "Think in Code" paradigm replaces dozens of file-read tool calls with a single sandboxed script that outputs only the relevant result, and routing enforcement is applied automatically across 17 supported platforms via MCP plus hook integrations. It is licensed under ELv2, distributed as an npm package and Claude Code plugin, and targets engineering teams using AI coding assistants in environments such as Claude Code, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible clients.

**Product Description Text**:
> cut Fable 5 token usage by rendering text context as images

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> pxpipe is a local proxy that lowers Claude Code (and compatible agent) costs through rendering bulky request context — system prompts, tool docs, and older chat history — as compact PNG images before they leave the host machine. Because image tokens are priced by pixel area rather than visible content, dense payloads (code, JSON, tool output) pack roughly 3.1 characters per image-token against ~1 character per text-token, and a calibrated profitability gate ensures only token-dense sections are imaged while sparse prose stays as text. The rewrite is lossy: byte-exact values such as hashes and IDs are preserved natively in a factsheet, and an escape hatch routes precision-critical subagents (e.g., `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-6`) through text-only paths. A dashboard at `127.0.0.1:47821/` exposes per-request savings, side-by-side text/image diffs, and live model chips; alternative `pxpipe warp` and `export` modes provide transparent shell-level wrapping and offline PNG generation for clients like Cursor. End-to-end Claude Code bills land 59–70% lower at current pricing, with SWE-bench Lite at 10/10 both arms and SWE-bench Pro at 14/19 (ON) vs 15/19 (OFF) on small-n pilots. The stack is TypeScript and Node (installed via `npx pxpipe-proxy` / `npm i -g pxpipe-proxy`), uses model-specific render profiles such as the 1568×728 / 312-column Claude profile, and ships with reproducible receipts under `eval/` and `docs/`.

It operates through three reflexive levers: a YAGNI-first code ladder that favors the smallest viable solution, prose compression that drops narration and hedging, and dense agent-to-agent handoff formats (compact JSON or ESON) that roughly halve transfer size with lossless recovery. Auto-intensity (lite/full/ultra) is chosen per-request with no reasoning overhead, and safety carve-outs protect validation, error handling, auth, secrets, migrations, and deletes from compression. It works across Claude (web and API), Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Cline, OpenClaw, oh-my-pi, Kiro, Kilo Code, and Hermes Agent, shipping as an always-on core with on-demand satellite skills (review, eco, gain, compress) and read-only subagents. A reproducible benchmark suite (`bench/`) covers 23 tasks across code, user-facing, and agent-to-agent tiers, evaluating output against Caveman and Ponytail baselines using paired Wilcoxon sign tests and a four-model judge panel; on Claude Opus results show 71% LOC reduction and 24% cost reduction at 100% test pass with zero failing cells.

Users configure and authenticate each upstream MCP server once in Toolport, and any AI client that supports MCP (Claude, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, and similar tools) can then reach them all through the same connection, reportedly reducing tool-related token usage by up to 90 percent. The gateway auto-detects locally configured MCP servers and exposes them uniformly, eliminating the need to repeat the same setup across multiple editors. A separate Teams edition adds a Docker-based self-hosted gateway with GitHub OAuth, intended for organizations that need shared access and centralized control.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Toolport is a free, open-source local gateway for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that consolidates many MCP servers behind a single endpoint, letting users configure and authenticate each upstream server once and then expose them all to any MCP-compatible AI client such as Claude, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, and Windsurf. It tackles the so-called "tool tax" by replacing the full catalog of upstream tool definitions with a small set of meta-tools that the agent searches on demand, cutting tool-related token usage by up to 90% while preserving task success rates. Security and governance are first-class concerns: API keys are kept in the operating system keychain rather than config files or the cloud, every tool is fingerprinted to flag definition changes ("rug pulls") and tool-poisoning attacks, and per-tool toggles plus a unified permission policy let users hide destructive tools fleet-wide. The app is distributed as a native desktop client for Windows, macOS, and Linux (MIT licensed) and adds cross-client management of agent rules and permission presets, with live observability for latency, errors, and audit logs. A separate Teams edition, offered free for up to five users, packages Toolport as a Docker-based self-hosted gateway with GitHub OAuth so organizations can share MCP servers centrally while keeping each user's secrets on their own machine.

**Product Description Text**:
> RTK's toolkit for building AI applications. RTK is an open-source framework from RTK AI that helps developers build AI-powered applications with reusable components and workflows

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> RTK (Rust Token Killer) is a CLI proxy designed to reduce LLM token consumption by intercepting shell commands and compressing their output before it reaches an AI agent's context. It solves the problem of bloated bash output consuming expensive context windows, achieving reductions of up to 90% on common development commands like `git status`, `cargo test`, `ls`, and `grep` through smart filtering, grouping, truncation, and deduplication strategies. The tool supports 100+ commands across file operations, Git, GitHub CLI, and major test runners (Jest, pytest, Go test, cargo test), with output transformed into compact formats such as tree listings with file counts, one-line commit logs, and failures-only test summaries. It integrates with popular AI coding agents including Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, and Codex via automatic hook-based command rewriting. Distributed as a single Rust binary with zero runtime dependencies and under 10ms overhead, RTK installs via Homebrew, curl, Cargo, or pre-built binaries for macOS, Linux, and Windows, making it ideal for developers using AI assistants who want to lower API costs and fit more code into limited context windows.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Files SDK is a unified JavaScript/TypeScript storage library that abstracts away the differences between cloud object and blob providers, letting application code call `upload`, `download`, `exists`, `copy`, `move`, `list`, and `signedUrl` through a single, consistent API. It ships adapters for S3 and S3-compatible services (R2, MinIO, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, DigitalOcean Spaces), Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, Vercel Blob, the local filesystem, and consumer providers like Dropbox, with each adapter as a tree-shakeable subpath and the native provider SDK as an optional peer dependency. Bodies are web-standard `Blob`, `File`, `ReadableStream`, `Uint8Array`, `ArrayBuffer`, or `string`, so no provider-specific types leak into caller code, while a `files.raw` escape hatch exposes the underlying native client for features the abstraction does not cover. A lazy `loadFiles` loader and a `FILES_SDK_PROVIDER` env var let Node.js tools pick a provider at runtime without bundling unused adapters. The same `Files` instance is also wrapped as ready-made tools for the Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI's Responses/Agents SDK, and Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, giving models a uniform way to browse and read bucket contents. Developers building multi-cloud, serverless, or AI-agent applications on Node, Bun, or edge runtimes benefit most, and the project is MIT-licensed with mocked unit tests by default plus opt-in `*.live.test.ts` suites gated by `LIVE_TESTS=1` and credentials.

The project supports installation via the open-source `skills` CLI across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi, Kiro, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, and dozens more, plus an npm package and a read-only MCP server for environments that prefer that interface. Frontend teams and individual developers working with modern React stacks who want AI assistants to suggest accurate, version-appropriate patterns rather than legacy APIs are the primary audience.

Researchers and engineers working on training, evaluating, or benchmarking LLM-based software engineering agents will find it especially useful, with support for integration with SWE-agent and GRPO-style reinforcement learning via SkyRL. **Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> TypeSafe Mario is an experimental harness that connects TypeSafe's Jev language model to Nintendo's original Super Mario Bros., allowing the model to play the game by issuing NES controller inputs based on structured telemetry rather than raw screenshots. A custom parser converts emulator RAM and runtime observations into compact, object-centric JSON describing Mario's motion, jump trajectory, nearby enemies, terrain geometry, reaction timing, recent control outcomes, and episode progress, which Jev uses to choose one of seven legal actions such as `right_run_jump` or `noop`. Each decision also runs two auxiliary judgments—a `Noul` estimating jump utility and a `Score` measuring immediate danger—exposing confidence and probability distributions for visualization without overriding Jev's choices. The package ships with CLI tools for previewing model inputs (`state-demo`), running World 1-1 with configurable decision cadence (`play`), and inspecting a live dashboard or headless benchmark, while every decision is logged to timestamped JSONL files for later analysis. Researchers and hobbyists interested in language-model agents, real-time decision systems, or NES emulation can use it as a reproducible testbed, provided they supply their own legally obtained ROM. The stack is Python 3.13 with a `gym-super-mario-bros` emulation backend, Pygame-based rendering, and standard tooling (`ruff`, `pytest`) for development.
